source.citation: Vincze O, Colchero F, Lemaître JF, Conde DA, Pavard S, Bieuville M, Urrutia AO, Ujvari B, Boddy AM, Maley CC, Thomas F, Giraudeau M. Cancer risk across mammals. Nature. 2022;601(7892):263-267

statement.value: We show that the phylogenetic distribution of cancer mortality is associated with diet, with carnivorous mammals (especially mammal-consuming ones) facing the highest cancer-related mortality. Moreover, we provide unequivocal evidence for the body size and longevity components of Peto’s paradox by showing that cancer mortality risk is largely independent of both body mass and adult life expectancy across species.

explanandum.value: Limited data available so far indicate that vertebrates do not face clear size-dependent cancer risks despite their size and longevity varying by orders of magnitude.

summary.value: They suggest that lifespan extension and larger body size jointly evolved with better anticancer mechanisms across mammals.

scope.value: Individuals in the husbandry module of ZIMS that were alive or born after 1 January 2010 and reached sexual maturity before or during the sampling period, with a date of birth recorded precisely or within 30 days, in species with postmortem pathological records for at least 20 adult individuals; species subject to domestication and their wild ancestors are excluded (110,148 individuals, 191 species). Neoplasia is recorded only as tumours that contributed to death, with no option to specify the cancer type.

text.value: A complete-case analysis is used, on the 11,840 individuals whose cause of death was specified together with the right-censored survivors. It assumes that a missing cause of death is missing at random; the authors had no reason to believe otherwise for this dataset, because postmortem examinations are routine and their results are equally likely to be entered whatever the pathology found.
text.basis_quote: However, here we performed a complete-case analysis, using only 11,840 individuals for which the cause of death was specified together with right-censored survivors. Complete-case analysis assumes that missingness in the cause of failure is random, but we had no reason to believe that this was not the case in our dataset. Postmortem examinations are routinely carried out on most recovered bodies in zoos, and once examinations are performed the results are equally likely to be entered in the database irrespective of the pathologies identified.

text.value: Both models are controlled for phylogenetic relatedness among species, with the scaling parameter of phylogenetic dependence set per model by likelihood ratio statistics; the PGLS models whose Pagel's lambda converged to a negative value were refitted with it fixed at 0.
text.basis_quote: Both models were controlled for phylogenetic relatedness among species, where the scaling parameter of phylogenetic dependence (that is, s2/Pagel’s λ in PGLMMs and PGLSs respectively) was set to the most appropriate values assessed by likelihood ratio statics in each model separately. PGLS models in which Pagel’s λ converged to negative values were refitted with Pagel’s λ fixed at 0.

text.value: Cancer is registered in the database only for deceased animals, and only if the inspecting veterinary pathologist considered it to be a factor that contributed to the individual's death.
text.basis_quote: Cancer is registered in this database only for deceased animals and only if the inspecting veterinary pathologist considered it to be a factor that contributed to the individual’s death.

text.value: Cancer mortality risk is estimated by two metrics, both the proportion of individuals dying of cancer: the simple cancer mortality risk (CMR), which relies solely on dead individuals and may therefore be biased, and the cumulative incidence of cancer mortality (ICM), which eliminates potential biases due to disregarding left-truncation and right-censoring.
text.basis_quote: Second, to estimate cancer mortality risk, we used two metrics, both estimating the proportion of individuals dying of cancer. We first calculated a simple measure of cancer mortality risk (hereafter CMR; that is, the ratio between the number of cancer-related deaths and the total number of individuals whose postmortem pathological records were entered in the database, n = 11,840), a measure adopted by earlier comparative studies15,17. This measure relies solely on dead individuals, ignoring the incomplete records of live animals, potentially introducing bias in cancer mortality estimates. Therefore, we also calculated the cumulative incidence of cancer mortality (hereafter ICM), a metric of cancer mortality risk eliminating potential biases due to disregarding left-truncation (that is, cancer before individuals enter the study) and right-censoring (individuals alive, thus with unknown fate at data extraction).

text.value: The two metrics agree: ICM is strongly consistent with CMR (Pearson correlation, r = 0.89, t = 25.14, df = 170, P < 0.0001). All models were nonetheless run with both, to test the consistency of the results.
text.basis_quote: ICM showed strong consistency with CMR (Pearson correlation test, r = 0.89, t = 25.14, df = 170, P < 0.0001). Nonetheless, all models were performed using both metrics to test for consistency in the results.

text.value: The effect of diet was tested only on the species with a non-zero cancer mortality risk.
text.basis_quote: The effect of diet was tested in PGLS regressions using only species with non-zero cancer mortality risks.

text.value: The proportion of dead individuals with postmortem pathological records is larger in larger species (Pearson's correlation r = 0.24, t = 3.35, df = 189, P = 0.001).
text.basis_quote: large species are considered of key importance for zoos, also reflected by the fact that the proportion of dead individuals with postmortem pathological records is larger in larger species (Pearson’s correlation: r = 0.24, t = 3.35, df = 189, P = 0.001)

text.value: ICM was computed only for the species in which survival is correctly estimated until old ages — those whose data allow age-specific survival to be estimated until the age at which only 10% of individuals survive — which this paragraph gives as 172 species.
text.basis_quote: For calculation of ICM, we included only species in which survival is correctly estimated until old ages (that is, data allowing the estimation of age-specific survival until the age at which only 10% of individuals are surviving, n = 172 species).

text.value: The probability of detecting cancer was modelled on 188 species for CMR and 141 for ICM, and non-zero cancer mortality risk on 141 species for CMR and 128 for ICM.
text.basis_quote: The probability of detecting cancer (CMR: n = 188; ICM: n = 141) (Extended Data Table 3 and Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5), as well as non-zero cancer mortality risk (CMR: n = 141; ICM: n = 128) (Extended Data Table 3 and Fig. 3), tended to decrease with larger body masses and to increase with longer life expectancies.

text.value: The interaction between body mass and longevity was tested in all four models and increased model fit in none of them, so it is not presented; the additive effect of the two is what the authors expected.
text.basis_quote: Given the expected additive effect of body mass and longevity, the interaction between body mass and longevity metrics was also tested in all four models (binomial and logistic regressions for CMR and ICM), but these interactions did not increase model fit in any case and are therefore not presented.

text.value: Species-specific adult life expectancies were calculated by survival modelling of the 110,148 individuals and represent average adult longevity in this sample, not a maximum reported lifespan.
text.basis_quote: First, to characterize species longevities, we used survival modelling (n = 110,148) and calculated species-specific adult life expectancies, representing average adult longevity in our sample

text.value: Three species of very low adult life expectancy were removed from the PGLS models for their high leverage; the models were also run on the entire dataset, with results the authors report as highly consistent.
text.basis_quote: PGLS models in which Pagel’s λ converged to negative values were refitted with Pagel’s λ fixed at 0. Three species (Lagurus lagurus, Cricetus cricetus and Dasyuroides byrnei) had been removed from the latter models, due to their high leverage caused by their very low adult life expectancy compared to the rest of the species and therefore concerns of strong influence of these points over model fit. Nonetheless, all models were performed using the entire dataset, and the results were highly consistent with and without the exclusions (Supplementary Table 4 and Extended Data Fig. 7).

text.value: Every cell division carries a risk of generating mutations, so organisms with large bodies, composed of more cells, and with extended longevities, having longer to accumulate mutations, should be more likely to develop cancer.
text.basis_quote: Given that every cell division carries a risk of generating mutations, organisms with large bodies (composed of more cells) and extended longevities (with a longer time to accumulate mutations) should be more likely to develop cancer

text.value: Diet information was obtained from a global diet dataset for terrestrial mammals.
text.basis_quote: Diet information was obtained from a global diet dataset for terrestrial mammals32, providing information on diet composition at four hierarchical levels of food items (never consumed, occasionally consumed, secondary food item, primary food item).

text.value: Order differences in cancer incidence were tested using standard linear regressions, with non-transformed CMR or ICM as the dependent variable and order as the sole explanatory factor, on the orders in which at least two species had an estimate.
text.basis_quote: Order differences in cancer incidence were tested using standard linear regressions, built using only taxonomic orders in which at least two species had their cancer incidence estimated. The model contained CMR or ICM (non-transformed) as dependent variables and order as the sole explanatory factor.

statement.value: Cancer is a prevailing source of mortality in many mammalian species across the phylogeny, at least in managed populations: the simple cancer mortality risk ranged from 0% (47 of 191 species) to 57.14% and exceeded 10% in 41 species.

statement.value: Oncogenic phenomena are quasi-universal across mammals: with adequate sampling cancer is likely to be detected in all mammals.

statement.value: Cancer mortality risk shows strong phylogenetic signal across mammals, driven mostly by Carnivora, whose risk is significantly higher than that of Primates or Artiodactyla; Artiodactyla is the least cancer-prone order despite its many large-bodied species.

modality.basis_quote: reveal substantial differences in cancer mortality across major mammalian orders

statement.value: Some members of the order Artiodactyla, besides rodents, are particularly cancer-resistant: cancer mortality risk in this dataset was lowest among ruminants.

modality.basis_quote: Our results further emphasize the fact that some members of the order Artiodactyla, besides rodents, are particularly cancer-resistant.

statement.value: Across mammal species, cancer mortality risk is not significantly associated with body mass: the estimated effect is slightly negative, about a 2.8–2.9% decrease in cancer risk per doubling of body weight, and body mass accounts for 0.78% of the cross-species variance in the simple cancer mortality risk as a partial coefficient of determination.

modality.basis_quote: these results provide the largest-scale and most robust support to the body size and life expectancy components of Peto’s paradox in mammals

statement.value: Across mammal species, cancer mortality risk increases only minimally and non-significantly with adult life expectancy: about 24.7–25.2% per doubling of adult life expectancy, which accounts for 2.94% of the variance in the simple cancer mortality risk as a partial coefficient of determination.

modality.basis_quote: these results provide the largest-scale and most robust support to the body size and life expectancy components of Peto’s paradox in mammals

statement.value: The results suggest that lifespan extension and larger body size jointly evolved with better anticancer mechanisms across mammals.

modality.basis_quote: They suggest that lifespan extension and larger body size jointly evolved with better anticancer mechanisms across mammals.

statement.value: The article reads its results as highlighting a key role of life-history evolution in shaping cancer resistance across mammals.

modality.basis_quote: These results highlight the key role of life-history evolution in shaping cancer resistance and provide major advancements in the quest for natural anticancer defences.

statement.value: In phylogenetic regressions controlling for longevity and body mass, mammals whose natural diet frequently includes mammalian prey have significantly higher cancer mortality risk than mammals that rarely or never consume other mammals; consumption of vertebrate but not invertebrate prey is associated with higher risk, and an animal-based diet as such is not. The authors read this as a probably complex, maybe indirect evolutionary link, to be interpreted with caution.

modality.basis_quote: We show that the phylogenetic distribution of cancer mortality is associated with diet

statement.value: Pathogen-driven oncogenesis might have a considerable role in shaping cancer mortality risk in mammals: that mammals consuming other mammals appear to have the highest cancer risk of all diet categories is consistent with a pathogenic origin, because host jumps of pathogens are most likely between phylogenetically close prey and predator species.

modality.basis_quote: These results suggest that pathogen-driven oncogenesis might have a considerable role in shaping cancer mortality risk in mammals

claim_or_ref.text: Bio-magnification is the source of the elevated cancer risk among Carnivora.

value.unresolved_reason: The article finds it less likely because risk is not associated with invertebrate, fish, reptile or bird prey, but says the few species primarily eating these prey do not allow definitive conclusions.

claim_or_ref.text: The high cancer risk of carnivorous animals is related to their low microbiome diversity.
The high cancer risk of carnivorous animals is related to limited physical exercise under human care or to other aspects of their physiology.
The diet result is biased by alterations in the diet of housed carnivores.

value.unresolved_reason: The article says a lack of such bias should be confirmed by studying natural populations.

claim_or_ref.text: A high-fat, low-fibre diet, a known risk factor for carcinogenesis, explains the elevated cancer risk in Carnivora.

value.unresolved_reason: Stated at p[16]; this list carries one locator for all its elements. The article does not return to it explicitly; it finds that species with animal-based diets have cancer mortality risks comparable to species that rarely or never consume animals.

value.question: Do cancer patterns in zoo animals, whose diet, health, mortality factors, environment and biological functions are strongly controlled by humans, hold in wild populations, for which data on cancer incidence with ages and demographic histories are still out of reach?
value.consequence: The claims stand for managed populations; the natural incidence of malignancies is not described.

value.question: How much cancer goes unrecorded? Necropsies are likely to reveal most solid tumours, but benign tumours, liquid tumours such as leukaemia and early-stage cancers are unlikely to be recorded.
value.consequence: The cancer incidences estimated here are conservative.

value.question: Are more charismatic species subject to more frequent or more detailed necropsies?
value.consequence: The authors cannot exclude it, and argue it is unlikely to be a major source of bias: a charisma effect would predict a larger cancer risk in large mammals, the opposite of the non-significant negative body mass effect they find.

value.question: Which cancer types make up the recorded neoplasia? The database records tumours that contributed to death with no option to specify the type or other details.
value.consequence: No claim of this card is about a cancer type.

value.observation: Limited data available so far indicate that vertebrates do not face clear size-dependent cancer risks although their size and longevity vary by orders of magnitude (Peto’s paradox); most earlier estimates and analyses of this had considerable limitations, among them small sample sizes, missing information on the age distribution of cancer, data heterogeneity, and no control for phylogenetic relatedness; and the effect of longevity was generally tested with the much-debated metric of maximum reported lifespan, where prevalence is expected to correlate with life expectancy instead.
Managed populations of Carnivora have a high cancer risk.
Cancer cases are rarely reported in ruminants.

value.finding: High cancer risk in managed populations of Carnivora has previously been reported.
value.current_interpretation: Hormonal contraception (for example, progestins) and pregnancy postponement in zoo carnivores, both significant risk factors for certain cancers in humans as well as in non-domestic felids, may explain it.
value.proposed_interpretation: Cancer mortality risk shows no sex bias in Carnivora, although hormonal contraception is usually given to females, so the high risk is unlikely to be driven solely by reproductive management in zoo populations.

value.new_question: Do pathogens drive the cancers of mammals, in particular of species that eat other mammals?
value.why_not_askable_today: Proving the oncogenic properties of pathogens is notoriously difficult.
value.enabling_method: A search for pathogens in various cancer types.

value.new_question: How are tumour-suppressing mechanisms distributed across the mammalian phylogeny? The article states at p[31] that a considerable gap remains in knowledge of the taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity and distribution of those mechanisms.
value.why_not_askable_today: A considerable gap remains in knowledge of the taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity and distribution of tumour-suppressing mechanisms: the studies that demonstrated them were done mostly in rodents and in very large animals.
value.enabling_method: The article offers its own results as the foundation: information on the generality and frequency of oncogenic phenomena across the mammalian phylogeny, drawn from the resources zoos provide for studies of cancer in wildlife.

value.new_question: Can other mammalian groups, especially Artiodactyla, serve as informative model organisms in cancer research? The article proposes it at p[23], on the strength of the low cancer mortality risk it finds among ruminants.
value.why_not_askable_today: The search for mechanisms of cancer resistance has been conducted mostly in rodents and in very large animals, and a considerable gap remains in knowledge of the taxonomic and phylogenetic distribution of tumour-suppressing mechanisms.
value.enabling_method: Study of the cancer-resistant Artiodactyla the article identifies.

value.outcome: A possible contribution to knowledge of natural anticancer mechanisms.
value.beneficiaries_or_system: Natural anticancer mechanisms that could potentially be harnessed for medical use; and, as the next step the article attaches to understanding cross-species variation of cancer vulnerability, animal health and welfare.
value.causal_bridge: It is often postulated that natural selection on large size or extended longevity is inherently inseparable from the evolution of anticancer defences; on that postulate, knowledge gained from investigating Peto's paradox might largely contribute to knowledge of natural anticancer mechanisms.

value.justification: The claims rest on zoo data, which give exceptionally high resolution on demography and cause of death for a wide range of species, with necropsy routinely performed on most deceased animals. Data on cancer incidence in wild populations, which would be indispensable to describe natural incidences, are still far from reach.

cheapest_test.text: Estimate cancer-related mortality from routine necropsies of deceased zoo animals of known demography, across a wide range of species.

source_ref.limitation: The article itself; its full text is not in this repository.

value.note: The claims of this card are made in this article; the date is the publication date in the Europe PMC record. Peto’s paradox itself was first formulated by Sir Richard Peto, cited at paragraph 7 as references 6 and 14, and the article dates it in its own reference list: reference 6 is "Peto, R. in Origins of Human Cancer Vol 45 (eds. Hiatt, H. et al.) 1403-1428 (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, 1977)". A locator in OHF 1.0 cannot name a reference-list entry, so that date is read from the bytes the card cites without being addressable in them; the errata records it.

lines.quote: We argue that decreased cancer rates need not necessarily be a result of a direct selection for mechanisms specifically/uniquely involved in tumor suppression. Instead, we suggest a more parsimonious connection, where selection acts on a more general trait of enhanced tissue maintenance in species with slower life histories (i.e. larger body mass and longer lifespan)

study_system.value: species with slower life histories, as the argument addresses them

lines.quote: the authors demonstrated that the somatic mutation rate is inversely proportional to lifespan in 16 mammalian species

study_type.value: commentary reporting the whole-genome result of another study (Cagan et al.), as this paragraph states it

value.note: This paragraph attributes the finding to another study: "In a recent study published in Nature, Alex Cagan, Adrian Baez-Ortega and colleagues found that many mammalian species present a similar somatic mutational load at the end of life", and states the inference as a possibility: "These data may suggest that mutational burden predicts mortality". It also states what the finding does not reach: "The mutational burden is independent of lifetime and body mass, only varying by a relatively small fold change among species."

Nothing in this card is retracted. The retraction status of its four sources is a different question, and it was checked: four status calls on 2026-10-21, all none_found (search-log.jsonl, and added.source_verification.metadata_check for the article itself).

The article states its conditions in one methods paragraph, which this card carries whole in core.scope. It declares no separate typed context, and splitting the paragraph into typed qualifiers would be the converter's reading, not the authors'.
The fifteen assumptions are the authors' own statements, quoted in their basis quotations. The converter made no assessment of its own about them, so there is none to record.
The ten atoms are siblings. The article builds no hierarchy among its claims, and a parent the converter chose would be a structure the article does not have.
No atom is a compound of other atoms, so none carries an operator.

Every atom holds in the scope the card states, except a_diet, whose context is narrower: the diet variable comes from a global diet dataset for terrestrial mammals (p[39]), so the diet results do not cover the marine species of the 191. The restriction is carried in as_terrestrial_diet rather than in a context_override, because the field takes a scope object and what the article states is a property of the dataset, not a redefined population; this is named in the report.

The article states no result that would count against its claims. The field is still empty rather than filled from the literature: the card carries seven lines whose direction is disputes, among them Butler et al.'s finding on body size (butler_size, p[16]), and those are results that bear against atoms of this card - but a falsification condition is a statement of what would count as refutation, which neither the article nor those works makes, and writing one would be the converter's own criterion. The disputing lines are where a reader should look, and the report says so.

The authors claim novelty ("unequivocal empirical evidence for Peto's paradox is lacking", p[2]) but state no bounded new-versus-shared content, and this field needs retained search or review evidence for that split. The search layer measured where the article stands (196 citing works, 16 attached responses, SEARCH-20261021.md); it does not establish what is new in it.

The article gives cancer mortality risk per species, not a rate in one explicit reference class with its denominator; the 0%-to-57.14% range and the 41-species count are claims of the card, in a_frequent, and not a base rate for the hypothesis.

The card carries no mechanism step, so there is no step whose interior is a black box. The article does state a route — raw meat exposes carnivores to pathogens that can drive oncogenic transformation, and a host jump is likeliest between phylogenetically close prey and predator — but it states it as arguable and offers no groundable entity: in its whole body it names no pathogen taxon, no gene and no molecule, so a typed step would need a subject and an object the converter invented. The route is carried as the atom a_pathogen with modality speculative, and the missing typed step is recorded in completeness.missing_for_next.

The article names no molecular target of its own. TP53 appears only in an added source (Butler p[7], itself citing Sulak et al. 2016) and the article names no gene anywhere in its body: "TP53", "p53", "MDM2" and any form of "duplicat" occur zero times in PMC8755536.
The prediction is about natural populations of Mammalia; a clade has no strain or line.
The prediction names no sex. The article tested sex separately, in Carnivora, and found no bias (e_sex_bias_null), which is a result and not a restriction on this prediction.
The prediction is a cross-species contrast of mortality risk, not a follow-up from a starting age; the article states none.
The article states no age at assessment for the prediction; its own estimates are age-controlled across whole adult populations.
The prediction names no site; the article says only that it would be tested in natural populations.

The article states no spatial scale for the prediction.
The article states no temporal scale for the prediction.

The contrast is stated inside predictions[0].direction (frequent mammal-eaters against species that rarely or never eat mammals); the article names no separate comparator group.
An observational cross-species contrast has no control reference, and the article names none.
There is no control to rate, and the converter will not rate one that does not exist.
The article does not say whether a higher value of cancer mortality risk is the desired or the undesired direction; it reports the contrast without an orientation.

The search layer found no dataset of cancer mortality in natural mammal populations with diet that could test the prediction without new sampling; the article says such data are "still far from our reach".
The prediction is novel, so there is no known result it was fitted to.

The INDRA epistemics flag marks a statement extracted as a hypothesis rather than a result. Every line here is a reported result of its own source, and the authors' confidence is carried where a reader expects it, in each atom's modality with the hedge quoted.

No line reports a negated statement. The measured nulls (e_animal_diet_null, e_sex_bias_null, e_biomagnification_null, e_two_zero_species) are findings in their own right, with their direction toward the target atom stated, not negations of another line.

Only one passage of the six sources states an interval (Butler p[18], a 95% CI for longevity in amphibians and squamate reptiles). One line with an interval and twenty without would read as a property of the evidence rather than of the reporting, so none is typed, and the interval stands in that line's own paragraph.

What each analysis was is already said in the line's study_type, which the entailment pass checks against the same passage. A second typed field saying it again would be checked against the same sentence twice without adding anything a reader could not read there.

Evidence strength is an assessment, and the converter makes only the two assessments it can ground: indirectness, from the distance between the study and the claim, and risk of bias, from a published reanalysis. It will not score strength on a scale the standard deliberately does not define.

Checked and recorded elsewhere, not withheld: four status calls on 2026-10-21 found no retraction, correction or expression of concern for any of the six sources (all none_found, search-log.jsonl), and the article's own Crossref check is in added.source_verification.metadata_check. The per-line field is a value bound to a passage of a source; a registry's "no notice" answer is not a passage of any of these four documents, so OHF 1.0 has nowhere to bind it.

No line is a replication of another. Dujon et al. reanalyse the article's own dataset, which is why e_dujon_reanalysis and e_dujon_longevity carry the same independence group as the article's own lines rather than a replication record.
The card cites four works, and each one is an added source with its own locators; evidence.references holds no entry, so there is no identifier to record. The empty list is named in the report.

The counts exist and are not in the card: every call is in search-log.jsonl with the sha256 of every response, five query families run twice on two services and in two sort orders, 196 citing works counted of which 31 are on the card's axis by title, 16 attached responses, 105 similar candidates narrowed to 25. The counts of calls and of lines are in the report, with the sha256 of the log as it stood at handover, because the log keeps growing while the conversion runs - the entity lookups write to it too - and a count written into the card would be stale by the next run. Of the sixteen responses attached to the article (call cf907c137f94) the card uses four: Lynch PMC12002202, Compton PMC12088420, Pepke PMC12018762 and Abplanalp & Rieger PMC9374720. Butler PMC11892590 is also on the card but is not one of the sixteen: it is a citing research article, reached by the cited_by calls d41a9560ce0d and 6960ba101ffb, and an earlier version of this reason counted it among the responses, which the log contradicts. The passage hedges ('need not necessarily', 'we suggest') and disputes only direct selection for cancer-specific mechanisms while accepting that reduced cancer rates accompany larger body mass and longer lifespan, so it qualifies rather than disputes the joint-evolution statement.

The passage grounds only the lifespan half of the statement (mutation rate inversely proportional to lifespan); it states that mutational load is independent of body mass and offers no evidence that larger body size jointly evolved with better anticancer mechanisms.

The three quotations are verbatim and do show secondhand attribution and a hedged inference, but the passage gives no grounds for grading risk of bias as "high" and the third quoted sentence states a positive finding rather than what the finding does not reach.
